toyota_summary:
The EU moved to restrict steel imports today to counter Chinese and American competition, a measure that will raise costs for automakers sourcing materials across the bloc. Steel represents a significant input cost for vehicle production, and tariff walls around European suppliers will force manufacturers to either pay more or shift sourcing—both options squeeze margins in an industry already fighting through a transition to electric vehicles. Watch whether the auto industry lobbies successfully to carve out an exemption or preferential rate on steel used in EV production.

The USMCA trade agreement between the United States, Canada, and Mexico completed its first major review on July 1st, exposing tensions over labor standards and content rules that directly affect where automakers can build vehicles. Higher domestic-content requirements or stricter labor enforcement could push manufacturers to consolidate North American production, raising capital costs and reshaping regional supply chains. The bloc will complete negotiations by next year—any tightening of rules now is a signal to watch.

Four EU member states pressed Brussels this week to accelerate approval of self-driving cars on European roads. The push reflects a geopolitical calculation: whoever moves fastest on autonomous vehicles controls both the technology market and data advantage, and delay amounts to ceding ground to Chinese competitors already deploying fleets at scale. Look for the Commission to issue guidance on autonomous vehicle testing by autumn.
